# Results — Study 673 (T3, Tillson) on real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). One recipe — Tim Tillson's
T3(14, v=0.7) price-cross rule (long when close > T3, flat otherwise), entered with one
execution lag (position formed on the close of *t* earns the return of *t+1*), net of
one-way costs × NAV — raced against **buy-and-hold** and against the two "dumb" MAs it
claims to beat, an **SMA(14)** and an **EMA(14)** rule (same nominal N), plus a **T3-slope
timer** and a **volume-factor (v) robustness sweep**, on a basket of five liquid US tapes.
All series are **total-return** (`auto_adjust=True`); all Sharpe figures are net and
excess-of-cash (rf = 0 here, so net = excess). As-of **2026-06-30** (last complete
calendar month; last bar 2026-06-30). Headline tape **SPY: n = 8,411 daily bars
(~33.3 yr)**.*

## The mechanism claim, checked first — does T3 actually "hug price" with less lag?

Before racing the crossover, we check the literal pitch: a deterministic +20% step (flat,
then held) and the mean tracking distance to price, T3(14, v=0.7) vs SMA(14) vs EMA(14).

| Diagnostic | T3 | SMA | EMA |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| Mean \|close − line\| / close, SPY | **1.881%** | 1.535% | 1.327% |
| Value 5 bars after a +20% step (price = 120.0) | **105.29** | 108.57 | **111.52** |

T3 tracks price **less** tightly than either "dumb" benchmark at the same nominal N, and
after a shock it is the **slowest** of the three to catch up — the opposite of "virtually
eliminates lag." The reason is structural, not a bug in our implementation: T3 nests the
generalized-DEMA correction three times, and by the third nesting the input to the
correction is already a doubly-smoothed series, not raw price — six stacked EMA stages of
smoothing dominate the algebraic lag-correction at the same N. Tillson's own writeup
compares T3 to a **DEMA/TEMA of the same N** (where it legitimately smooths away
DEMA/TEMA's overshoot); against a **plain SMA/EMA of the same N** — the comparison every
retail chart actually invites when you drop "length = 14" into any of the three — the
low-lag half of the pitch does not hold.

## The honest test — SPY, long/flat, net of 5 bps one-way cost

The fair question is not "does the T3 rule make money" (any long-biased rule does in a
33-year bull tape) but "does its **timing** beat just **holding**?" — measured as the
daily **active spread** (strategy net − buy&hold), tested with a Newey-West HAC
one-sample *t*.

| Strategy | Sharpe (net) | CAGR (net) | Max DD | active spread (bps/day) | HAC *t* | switches/yr | time in mkt |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **T3(14, v=0.7) cross** | **0.308** | **2.85%** | −55.6% | **−3.40** | **−4.03** | **31.9** | 60% |
| SMA(14) cross | 0.238 | 2.07% | −57.6% | −3.70 | −4.42 | 36.5 | 63% |
| EMA(14) cross | 0.267 | 2.40% | −48.0% | −3.57 | −4.22 | 38.3 | 65% |
| **Buy & hold** | **0.647** | **10.83%** | −55.2% | — | — | 0 | 100% |

- T3 timing **loses to buy-and-hold by 3.40 bps/day** at HAC *t* = **−4.03** —
  statistically significant, on the *wrong* side of zero. Sitting in cash through 40% of a
  bull market is the cost; T3's smoother line does not pay for it.
- The gross (cost = 0) spread is **−2.77 bps/day, HAC *t* = −3.31** — costs deepen the
  hole but are not the root cause; the timing itself underperforms.

## "Fewer false signals (whipsaws)?" — the literal claim, partly true

Unlike a fast/low-lag filter (e.g. the Hull MA, Study 432), T3's six EMA stages make it
genuinely **smoother**, and that shows up directly in the switch count:

| Rule | switches / yr | active spread *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| **T3(14, v=0.7)** | **31.9** | −4.03 |
| SMA(14) | 36.5 | −4.42 |
| EMA(14) | 38.3 | −4.22 |

T3 fires **12–17% fewer** position changes than either benchmark — and this holds on
**all five** basket tickers (below). The "cleaner crossovers" half of the pitch is real.
It just doesn't pay: the head-to-head active-spread *t* against SMA is **+0.97** and
against EMA is **+0.42** — T3's edge over the dumb MAs it claims to beat is **not
statistically distinguishable from zero**, so fewer whipsaws is not the same as a better
trading rule.

## Head-to-head — is T3 better than the plain MA it claims to beat?

| Comparison | mean diff (bps/day) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|
| T3 − SMA(14) | +0.30 | +0.97 |
| T3 − EMA(14) | +0.17 | +0.42 |

Both point estimates favor T3, both fail to clear *t* = 2. T3 is not measurably better or
worse than the plain MAs it is sold as an upgrade over — all three simply lose to holding.

## Permutation placebo — is the timing real, or just exposure?

Hold the realised T3 position path's block structure but circularly shift it against
returns (destroying the timing, keeping the turnover and net-long bias), 2,000 draws,
gross spread statistic:

| Quantity | Value |
|---|--:|
| Observed T3 spread | −2.77 bps/day |
| Placebo mean spread | −1.89 bps/day |
| One-sided *p* (placebo ≥ observed) | **0.927** |

92.7% of random re-timings of the *same* position path beat the real T3 timing. T3's
*actual* calls carry **negative** information on this tape, not positive — consistent with
the mechanism check above (it reacts to shocks slower than the benchmarks it under-turns).

## Cost sweep (SPY, T3(14, v=0.7))

| round-trip cost | net Sharpe | active spread (bps/day) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 0.0 bps (gross) | 0.451 | −2.77 | −3.31 |
| 2.0 bps | 0.394 | −3.02 | −3.60 |
| 5.0 bps | 0.308 | −3.40 | −4.03 |
| 10.0 bps | 0.165 | −4.04 | −4.73 |

The spread is negative before costs; there is no break-even cost that rescues it.

## Per-instrument (T3(14, v=0.7) long/flat, cost = 5 bps)

| Ticker | T3 Sharpe (net) | Buy&hold Sharpe | active spread (bps/day) | HAC *t* | switches/yr T3 / SMA / EMA |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|---|
| SPY  | 0.308 | 0.647 | −3.40 | −4.03 | 31.9 / 36.5 / 38.3 |
| QQQ  | 0.227 | 0.521 | −4.08 | −3.05 | 31.4 / 36.6 / 39.8 |
| AAPL | 0.621 | 0.623 | −3.49 | −1.99 | 29.6 / 33.1 / 35.7 |
| MSFT | 0.519 | 0.821 | −6.18 | −4.94 | 30.7 / 37.3 / 40.9 |
| XLE  | 0.219 | 0.428 | −3.26 | −2.17 | 31.0 / 36.6 / 42.4 |

**Five of five** instruments: negative active spread; **four of five** clear *t* ≤ −2 on
their own (AAPL is the closest to zero at *t* = −1.99, still negative). T3 fires the
fewest switches/yr of the three rules on **all five** tickers — the whipsaw-reduction
mechanism replicates; the profitability failure does too.

## Robustness — in/out-of-sample split (SPY, T3, cost = 5 bps)

| Half | T3 Sharpe (net) | Buy&hold Sharpe | active spread (bps/day) | HAC *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| First half (1993–2009) | −0.059 | 0.455 | −3.88 | −2.99 |
| Second half (2009–2026) | 0.759 | 0.872 | −2.86 | −2.59 |

T3 loses to buy-and-hold in **both** halves; the underperformance is not a single-regime
artefact.

## Long/short variant (SPY, cost = 5 bps, borrow 50 bps/yr)

Flipping to short when close < T3 makes it worse: net Sharpe **−0.288**, active spread
**−6.89 bps/day** at HAC *t* = **−4.08**. Shorting an upward-drifting index on a
lagging-by-construction line compounds the loss.

## T3-slope timer variant (SPY, N=14, v=0.7, cost = 5 bps)

The other half of the brief — long when T3 itself is rising, flat otherwise:

| Rule | Sharpe (net) | Buy&hold Sharpe | active spread (bps/day) | HAC *t* | switches/yr |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| T3-slope | 0.557 | 0.647 | −2.27 | −2.66 | 10.5 |

Far fewer switches (the slope only flips on genuine trend reversals in the heavily-smoothed
line), and the spread is smaller — but still negative and still clears *t* ≥ 2 in magnitude
against buy-and-hold. Smoother is not the same as *better*.

## Volume-factor (v) robustness sweep — Tillson's own tuning knob

| v | net Sharpe | active spread (bps/day) | HAC *t* | switches/yr |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0.1 | 0.455 | −2.79 | −3.28 | 20.5 |
| 0.3 | 0.366 | −3.15 | −3.66 | 24.0 |
| 0.5 | 0.338 | −3.29 | −3.84 | 28.5 |
| **0.7 (Tillson's default)** | **0.308** | **−3.40** | **−4.03** | **31.9** |
| 0.9 | 0.246 | −3.67 | −4.45 | 33.8 |

Every v from 0.1 to 0.9 produces a **negative, significant** active spread (HAC
*t* between −3.28 and −4.45) — the underperformance is not an artefact of one
hand-picked "volume factor." Lower v (closer to a plain triple-EMA) is milder but never
positive; higher v (more DEMA/TEMA-like extrapolation) is worse.

## Synthetic positive control — the machinery works when there's a trend to find

On a deterministic synthetic daily tape (`data.synthetic_panel`) with a *planted*
persistent regime-switching trend, the same T3 engine banks the edge — and stays inside
the null band (checked over 20 seeds, not one lucky stream) when no trend is planted:

| World | T3 active spread (bps/day) | HAC *t* | net Sharpe |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| null (edge=0), 20 seeds | — | mean *t* = **−0.21** (sd 1.05), \|t\|≥2 in **2/20** seeds | — |
| planted edge = 0.3 | +7.19 | **+5.76** | 1.57 |
| planted edge = 0.6 | +26.64 | **+16.12** | 4.98 |
| planted edge = 1.0 | +50.27 | **+21.35** | 8.24 |

The engine is a faithful trend detector: plant a real trend and T3 finds it and clears
*t* = 2 by a wide margin. The real-tape verdict is therefore a statement about the
**market** (daily equity returns don't hand a heavily-smoothed line enough persistent
trend to pay for its lag) — not a broken harness. *(A faithful-engine / power check only —
never cited in support of the real-tape stamp.)*

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** T3(14, v=0.7) timing's active spread vs buy-and-hold is **−3.40
  bps/day at HAC *t* = −4.03** on SPY (gross *t* = −3.31), negative on all five tapes
  (four of five individually *t* ≤ −2), in both sample halves, and across **every** volume
  factor v from 0.1 to 0.9. The permutation placebo gives *p* = 0.927 — the timing is
  *worse* than random. T3 does not add positive timing information on daily US equities.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Even gross, the rule trails buy-and-hold; net of costs it
  falls further behind, the long/short version is outright destructive, and there is no
  break-even cost.
- **"Genuinely lower-lag, cleaner crossovers"? — MIXED.** *Cleaner* is real: T3 fires
  12–17% fewer switches than SMA/EMA of the same N, on all five tickers. *Lower-lag* is
  **busted**: T3 tracks price less tightly (1.88% vs 1.53%/1.33%) and reacts to a shock
  slower than either "dumb" benchmark — the opposite of Tillson's own pitch when compared
  at the same nominal N. Neither half translates into a certifiable edge over the MAs it
  claims to beat (head-to-head *t* = 0.97 / 0.42).
